items.q: What is the non-invasive ultrasound investigation of choice for detecting moderate-to-severe fetal anemia in an Rh-isoimmunized pregnancy?
o: Doppler measurement of fetal middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA PSV)
Amniocentesis for spectrophotometric bilirubin measurement (Delta OD450)
items.exp: Doppler velocimetry of the fetal middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA PSV) is the non-invasive gold standard for detecting fetal anemia. Because anemia reduces blood viscosity and increases cardiac output, cerebral blood velocity increases. An MCA PSV > 1.5 multiples of the median (MoM) detects moderate-to-severe fetal anemia with > 95% sensitivity.
r: Correct. Fetal MCA peak systolic velocity Doppler > 1.5 MoM is the non-invasive test of choice for fetal anemia.
Incorrect. Delta OD450 amniocentesis (Liley chart) was the historical gold standard, now replaced by non-invasive MCA Doppler.
Incorrect. Umbilical artery Doppler assesses placental resistance in FGR, not fetal anemia.
Incorrect. Biophysical profile reflects acute acidemia, not fetal hemoglobin levels.
items.kp: Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA PSV) Doppler > 1.5 MoM is the gold standard for detecting fetal anemia.

items.q: At what threshold of maternal anti-D antibody titer (indirect Coombs test) is the risk of fetal hemolytic disease considered significant enough to initiate serial fetal MCA Doppler monitoring?
items.exp: The critical titer for maternal anti-D antibodies on indirect Coombs testing is typically 1:16 to 1:32 (or >= 15 IU/mL). Once the maternal titer reaches or exceeds this critical threshold, titers no longer correlate reliably with disease severity, and serial fetal middle cerebral artery Doppler monitoring must be initiated.
r: Correct. A titer of 1:16 to 1:32 is the established critical threshold trigger for fetal Doppler monitoring.
Incorrect. Titers <= 1:8 carry low risk of hydrops; retesting every 2-4 weeks is sufficient.
Incorrect. Waiting for 1:128 causes dangerous delay and risks fetal hydrops before detection.
Incorrect. 1:1 represents trace sensitization.
items.kp: A maternal anti-D indirect Coombs titer of 1:16 to 1:32 represents the critical threshold warranting fetal surveillance.

items.q: What is the standard standard prophylactic dose of intramuscular Anti-D immunoglobulin administered routinely to non-sensitized RhD-negative pregnant women at 28 weeks gestation?
items.exp: The standard prophylactic dose of Anti-D immunoglobulin administered routinely at 28 weeks gestation and within 72 hours of delivering an Rh-positive infant is 300 mcg (1,500 IU). A 300 mcg dose neutralizes up to 30 mL of fetal whole blood (or 15 mL of fetal red blood cells). In the UK, split doses of 100 mcg (500 IU) are sometimes used.
r: Correct. 300 mcg (1,500 IU) is the standard prophylactic Anti-D dose, neutralizing 30 mL of fetal blood.
Incorrect. 50 mcg is used for first-trimester sensitizing events (miscarriage < 12 weeks).
Incorrect. 1,000 mcg is excessive for routine prophylaxis.
Incorrect. 10 mcg is subtherapeutic.
items.kp: Standard Anti-D prophylaxis is 300 mcg (1,500 IU) IM, neutralizing up to 30 mL of fetal whole blood.

items.q: Which laboratory test is performed on maternal blood following traumatic placental abruption or difficult delivery to quantify the volume of fetomaternal hemorrhage and calculate the required extra dose of Anti-D immunoglobulin?
items.exp: The Kleihauer-Betke acid elution test quantifies fetomaternal hemorrhage by exposing maternal blood to an acid buffer. Adult maternal hemoglobin (HbA) elutes out, leaving ghost cells, while fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is acid-resistant and stains darkly. Counting the percentage of fetal cells allows calculation of fetomaternal hemorrhage volume to guide Anti-D dosing.
r: Correct. The Kleihauer-Betke test quantifies fetomaternal hemorrhage to determine the required Anti-D dose.
Incorrect. Direct antiglobulin test detects in vivo antibody coating on red blood cells.
Incorrect. Apt test differentiates fetal from maternal blood in vaginal bleeding (vasa previa).
Incorrect. Southern blot analyzes DNA fragments.
items.kp: The Kleihauer-Betke test quantifies fetomaternal hemorrhage to determine additional Anti-D immunoglobulin requirements.

items.q: What characterizes the packed red blood cells transfused during intrauterine fetal transfusion for severe fetal anemia?
o: Type O RhD-negative, CMV-negative, leukodepleted, irradiated, and cross-matched against maternal serum
Type AB RhD-positive fresh whole blood
Maternal autologous unwashed packed red cells
items.exp: Blood transfused to a fetus in utero must be: Type O RhD-negative (compatible with maternal and fetal antibodies); CMV-negative (preventing fetal viral infection); leukodepleted; irradiated (preventing fatal graft-versus-host disease in the immunocompromised fetus); tightly packed (hematocrit 75-80%); and cross-matched against maternal serum.
r: Correct. O-negative, CMV-negative, leukodepleted, irradiated packed red cells cross-matched with maternal blood are mandatory.
Incorrect. AB-positive blood would be immediately hemolyzed by maternal anti-D antibodies.
Incorrect. Maternal blood contains high titers of circulating anti-D antibodies.
Incorrect. Paternal blood expresses the foreign RhD antigen.
items.kp: Intrauterine blood transfusion requires O-negative, CMV-negative, irradiated, leukodepleted packed red cells.

items.q: How does alloimmunization against the Kell antigen (anti-Kell) differ clinically from Rhesus alloimmunization (anti-D)?
o: Anti-Kell causes severe fetal anemia primarily by suppressing erythroid progenitor cells in bone marrow, with lower antibody titers
Anti-Kell antibodies are IgM and cannot cross the placenta
items.exp: Unlike anti-D (which destroys mature circulating erythrocytes via splenic extravascular hemolysis), anti-Kell antibodies target Kell antigens expressed early on erythroid progenitor cells (CFU-E and BFU-E), causing direct immune destruction of bone marrow progenitors and severe reticulocytopenia. Consequently, severe fetal anemia can occur at very low antibody titers (>= 1:4).
r: Correct. Anti-Kell suppresses erythroid progenitor development in fetal marrow, causing severe anemia even at low titers.
Incorrect. Anti-Kell can cause profound, life-threatening fetal hydrops.
Incorrect. Anti-Kell is IgG and crosses the placenta efficiently.
Incorrect. Anti-Kell affects fetuses early in gestation.
items.kp: Anti-Kell causes fetal anemia primarily by destroying erythroid progenitor cells in bone marrow, causing hydrops at low titers.

items.q: What is the sonographic definition of hydrops fetalis?
o: Pathological fluid accumulation in at least two separate fetal compartments (e.g., ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, skin edema)
Isolated polyhydramnios with normal fetal anatomy
Severe fetal growth restriction with oligohydramnios
items.exp: Hydrops fetalis is defined sonographically by the presence of pathological fluid accumulation in at least two distinct fetal serous cavities or tissues, such as: fetal ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, or generalized skin edema (anasarca, subcutaneous thickening > 5 mm). It is frequently accompanied by placental thickening (> 4-6 cm) and polyhydramnios.
r: Correct. Fluid accumulation in at least two separate fetal compartments defines hydrops fetalis.
Incorrect. Isolated polyhydramnios does not meet the definition.
Incorrect. FGR with oligohydramnios is placental insufficiency, not hydrops.
Incorrect. Scalp edema alone in an isolated compartment is insufficient.
items.kp: Hydrops fetalis requires pathological fluid accumulation in at least two separate fetal compartments.

items.q: An RhD-negative non-sensitized primigravida undergoes chorionic villus sampling (CVS) at 11 weeks gestation. What is the recommended management regarding Anti-D prophylaxis?
o: Administer 50 mcg (or 250 IU) of Anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours of the procedure
Administer 1,000 mcg of Anti-D immunoglobulin immediately
No Anti-D is needed before 20 weeks gestation
Wait until 28 weeks to administer routine prophylaxis
items.exp: Chorionic villus sampling is an invasive intrauterine procedure that causes fetomaternal hemorrhage. In non-sensitized Rh-negative women undergoing sensitizing events in the first trimester (< 12 weeks), a minimum dose of 50 mcg (250 IU) of Anti-D immunoglobulin must be administered within 72 hours to prevent primary sensitization.
r: Correct. 50 mcg (250 IU) of Anti-D within 72 hours is recommended for first-trimester invasive procedures.
Incorrect. 1,000 mcg is inappropriately high for early first-trimester exposure.
Incorrect. Anti-D is mandatory following sensitizing events at any gestational age.
Incorrect. Delaying until 28 weeks allows primary maternal sensitization to occur.
items.kp: Anti-D immunoglobulin (50 mcg in first trimester) must be given within 72 hours of invasive intrauterine procedures.

items.q: Why is ABO incompatibility between an O-negative mother and an A-positive father partially protective against maternal RhD isoimmunization?
o: Naturally occurring maternal anti-A and anti-B antibodies destroy fetal RBCs in maternal circulation before RhD antigen recognition occurs
ABO antigens mask and physically cover RhD antigens on the erythrocyte membrane
Anti-A antibodies bind and neutralize maternal Rh receptors
RhD antigens are not expressed on Type A red cells
items.exp: In ABO-incompatible gestations (e.g., group O mother carrying a group A, Rh-positive fetus), pre-existing maternal anti-A antibodies rapidly bind and hemolyze fetal red cells upon entering the maternal circulation. These coated fetal cells are swiftly cleared by maternal liver Kupffer cells before the maternal splenic immune system can process and recognize the RhD antigen, reducing the sensitization rate by > 75%.
r: Correct. Pre-existing maternal ABO isohemagglutinins rapidly clear fetal cells before RhD immune recognition.
Incorrect. ABO antigens do not physically mask RhD surface proteins.
Incorrect. Anti-A antibodies do not bind Rh receptors.
Incorrect. RhD antigens are expressed independently of ABO blood types.
items.kp: ABO incompatibility partially protects against Rh sensitization because maternal anti-A/B antibodies rapidly destroy fetal cells.

items.q: What is the targeted post-transfusion fetal hematocrit following intrauterine umbilical vein blood transfusion for severe fetal anemia?
items.exp: During intrauterine blood transfusion, the volume of transfused packed red cells is carefully calculated to raise the fetal hematocrit to a normal physiological target of 40% to 45%. Exceeding this threshold (> 50-60%) increases blood viscosity and risks fetal cerebral thrombosis or acute circulatory overload.
r: Correct. A target fetal hematocrit of 40% to 45% restores oxygen delivery without hyperviscosity.
Incorrect. 60% to 65% creates hyperviscosity and vascular compromise.
Incorrect. 20% to 25% represents persistent severe anemia.
Incorrect. 80% is dangerously hyperviscous.
items.kp: Intrauterine blood transfusion targets a post-procedure fetal hematocrit of 40% to 45%.
